title: Your raga
hookLine: after a whole block of moods, some listeners find one raga that feels like home, and a line in Sri Rag's var says what makes a raga worth it

cards: Some people come alive before sunrise, with the kettle and the dark window. Others are only themselves after dinner, with the lamps on. Some love a heavy morning with work in it; some wait all year for spring.
It just turned out to be home. After weeks walking through the ragas of the Guru Granth Sahib, one mood after another, some listeners find that one of them has quietly become theirs.

teach.b: Lay out a few of the rooms on this road. Kedara at dusk, tender as the light goes. Bhairao, the serious morning, opening with nothing happens outside you.
Basant, where spring is always present. Kalyan in the evening, with a bee that comes back again and again. Prabhati at daybreak, with the Name as an ornament.
Jaijavanti, where the ragas end: remember, this is your work. Each one put a mood around the same Word. Now a line from the Granth itself about ragas.
In the var of Sri Rag, Guru Amar Das writes, in paraphrase: among the ragas, Sri Rag stands high, if through it one comes to love the True One. Hear the condition. If.

teach.h: THE WORTH IS IN THE LOVE.
teach.b: The raga's worth isn't in the notes alone; it's in what the singing does to the heart.
A raga that leaves you cold hasn't done its work for you yet.
A raga that turns you toward the One has. That makes my raga a modest claim. It doesn't say this raga beats the others.

It says: this is where, for now, the love arrives most easily for me. Tradition gives ragas their hours and seasons, and the hymns inside them say what they say. But the listener is part of the music too.
Your hour of the day, your season, the mood you live in most, may lead you to one raga first. And the Granth's line suggests the test: not which one sounds best, but which one leaves you nearer.

how: Listeners of kirtan often come to love particular ragas and particular ragis; in the gurdwara, the raga sung usually follows the hymn's heading and the time of day.

o: the raga where, for now, your heart comes nearest the One
the raga played loudest at festival time
the raga a Sikh is assigned at birth by the family

p: stands high, if it brings love

s: the Granth says a raga is worth it only for its notes
Guru Amar Das ties Sri Rag's worth to coming to love the True One.
'my raga' means this raga is better than the others
it means where, for now, the love arrives most easily for you.
the line about Sri Rag comes from the var of Sri Rag
Guru Amar Das writes it in a salok there.

games.q: Guru Amar Das is about to say Sri Rag stands high among the ragas. what does he add?
o: because its notes are the hardest.
if through it one comes to love the True One.
because it comes first in the book.
games.why: the line puts a condition on it: the raga's worth is in the love it brings.

practice: Let the ragas on this road pass slowly through your mind, the dusk one, the serious morning, spring, evening, dawn, the last raga, and notice which one your breath settles into; if none does, let the hour of the day that feels most like home be your guide.

When one rises, say its name once, silently. If you pray, hold it as Guru Amar Das's line suggests, as a way toward love of the True One; if you don't, let the name be a small marker of where you feel at home.

wordCard.voice: Your raga. The one mood of the Granth's music where, for now, you come nearest; Guru Amar Das says a raga is worth it if through it one comes to love the True One. Today's word.

orig.note: raga: the heading word above each section of the Granth's hymns.

carryVoice: Your line: my raga. It names where, for now, the love arrives most easily. Thanks for listening with me.

sources.ref: Sri Rag ki Var, salok Mahala 3, 'Raga vich Sriragu hai je sach dhare piar', Ang 83
